items.title: Focus Question: How does a CD produce a rainbow effect?

body.html: A CD's track spacing is 𝑑= 1.60 𝜇m. We want to explain the colors and estimate the first-order angles for violet (400 nm) and red (700 nm).
The tracks act as a reflection grating, 𝑚𝜆= 𝑑sin𝜃.
Each wavelength of white light has a bright maximum at its own angle, sin𝜃= 𝜆/ 𝑑.

answer.html: The spiral track is a reflection diffraction grating. Constructive interference happens at a different angle for each wavelength, so white light fans out into a spectrum from about 14.5° (violet) to 25.9° (red) in first order.

check.html: Violet appears at the smaller angle and red at the larger angle, as in the rainbow on a CD.

items.title: Get It? (p. 457): At the first dark band of a single slit of width 𝑤, what is the path difference between waves from the top edge and from the center of the slit, and what type of interference results?

answer.html: The path difference is 𝜆/ 2, so the waves arrive half a wavelength out of phase and interfere destructively. Every wavelet from the top half has a partner in the bottom half separated by 𝑤/ 2 that cancels it, which makes a dark band. The waves from the two edges differ by a full 𝜆.

items.title: Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question (Lesson 2): What information from this lesson helps explain why the blue of a Morpho butterfly wing shifts as you tilt it?

answer.html: Light bent around tiny structures spreads out (diffraction), and light from many closely spaced, regular features overlaps and interferes (grating). Different colors have constructive interference at different angles, so structures with spacing near the wavelength of light split white light into colors that change with viewing angle. The wing scale ridges act like a grating and multilayer reflector, so the reinforced color changes as you tilt the wing.

answer.html: A series of narrow, bright violet lines, equally spaced, with wide dark regions between them (brightest at the center), repeated symmetrically on both sides. The more slits, the narrower and brighter the lines.

check.html: This is the "diffraction grating pattern": the bright maxima sit where 𝑑sin𝜃= 𝑚𝜆, and there are weak minor peaks between them.

items.title: 29 (Critical thinking): A technician is handed an unlabeled optical element. When she views a white lamp through it she sees a white central image, with a complete spectrum on each side of it, violet nearest the center, and a second weaker spectrum farther out on each side. Is the element a prism or a grating? How can you tell the two apart?

answer.html: It is a grating. A grating gives (i) a white central image at 𝑚= 0 with spectra on both sides, (ii) repeated spectra in higher orders, and (iii) violet nearest the center and red farthest, with colors spaced almost evenly in angle. A prism gives one spectrum only, with red bent least and violet most, and no repeated orders and no white center. A single spectrum means a prism; repeated spectra on both sides of a white central line mean a grating.

check.html: The orders arise from 𝑚𝜆= 𝑑sin𝜃, which has multiple solutions; a prism has only one refraction angle per color.

Blue wavelengths satisfy the constructive condition over a wide range of angles, while the irregular heights spread the effect so the blue does not vanish with a small tilt. Pigment is not needed.

items.title: Focus Question: How do DVDs produce a rainbow effect?

body.html: The tracks of a DVD are closely spaced (about 740 nm apart), so the surface acts as a reflection grating: 𝑚𝜆= 𝑑sin𝜃.
Each wavelength of white light has a bright maximum at its own angle, sin𝜃= 𝜆/ 𝑑. Violet appears at a smaller angle than red, so the colors spread out into a spectrum.

answer.html: The spiral track acts as a reflection diffraction grating. Constructive interference occurs at a different angle for each wavelength, so white light is split into a rainbow.

answer.html: 𝑥<sub>obj</sub> ≈2.2 × 10<sup>10</sup> m

check.html: The angle is 1.22𝜆/ 𝐷= 2.8 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>7</sup> rad (0.058 arcsecond). The separation is about 0.15 AU (1 AU is 1.5 × 10<sup>11</sup> m), so Hubble could resolve the two stars even if they were much closer together than Earth is to the Sun.

items.title: 27 (Which grating has more lines per millimeter)

body.html: sin𝜃= 𝑚𝜆/ 𝑑; larger angle means smaller spacing 𝑑.
Same red laser, same 𝜆. The first grating spreads the dots farther (larger 𝜃), so its 𝑑 is smaller. Lines per millimeter is 1 / 𝑑, so a smaller 𝑑 means more lines.

answer.html: The first grating (the one with the more widely spread dots) has more lines per millimeter.

check.html: Consistent with 𝜆= 𝑑sin𝜃.

items.title: 28 (First-order dark bands, Figure 22)

question.html: From Figure 22: slit width 𝑤= 0.080 mm, distance to screen 𝐿= 68.0 cm (printed 68.0 cm), 𝜆= 546 nm.

body.html: The first-order dark bands on each side of the center are 𝑥<sub>1</sub> from the center, so the separation is the central band width 2𝑥<sub>1</sub> = 2𝜆𝐿/ 𝑤.

answer.html: 9.3 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> m = 9.3 mm

check.html: A fraction of a centimeter, a reasonable central band for a slit of 0.08 mm.

items.title: 29 (Critical thinking: prism or grating)

answer.html: Examine the spectrum from white light. A grating gives (i) a white central image at 𝑚= 0 with spectra on both sides, repeated in higher orders, (ii) violet nearest the center and red farthest, and (iii) colors spaced almost evenly with angle. A prism gives one spectrum only, with red bent least and violet most, and no repeated orders or white center. So if you see repeated spectra on both sides of a white central line, it is a grating; one spectrum is a prism.

check.html: The orders arise from 𝑚𝜆= 𝑑sin𝜃, which has multiple solutions; a prism has only one refraction angle per color.

items.title: Explanation: The petal surface has a row of tiny ridges whose spacing is about the wavelength of light,

question.html: with irregular heights and spacings. Light reflecting from different ridges has path differences that vary from place to place. Short wavelengths (blue and ultraviolet) are diffracted and scattered strongly at certain angles, while the irregularity makes the effect spread over a wide range of angles. The more variable the ridges, the stronger the blue halo, which bees can see.

answer.html: A diagram like the one above with a short note: ridges spaced near the wavelength of light diffract light; the disorder spreads blue/UV light into a halo around the flower.
